museums.content_summary: The **Anna Maria Island Historical Museum** offers a fascinating glimpse into the rich history of Anna Maria Island, showcasing its charming past through engaging exhibits. Located in a historic schoolhouse, this museum is perfect for those eager to uncover the island's intriguing stories and heritage.
museums.content_description:
Nestled in a quaint corner of *Anna Maria*, the **Anna Maria Island Historical Museum** brings to life the island's history through an immersive experience. Housed in a lovingly restored schoolhouse dating back to the 1920s, this museum provides an inviting atmosphere that draws visitors into the enchanting tales of the island’s past. From the early pioneers to the vibrant fishing community, every exhibit tells a story of resilience, growth, and the island's transformation into a beloved vacation destination.

Inside, visitors can explore a variety of collections epitomizing Anna Maria’s unique charm. Artifacts ranging from historic photographs and nautical relics to vintage fishing gear offer an authentic glimpse into daily life on the island. Each exhibit is curated thoughtfully to engage visitors of all ages, allowing families to connect with history in a meaningful way. A notable highlight is the collection of artifacts from the *Cortez Fishing Village*, which sheds light on the area’s longstanding heritage as a working waterfront.

The museum’s friendly and knowledgeable staff enhance the experience with guided tours that provide deeper insights into the exhibits. Whether you are a history buff or simply seeking an enjoyable outing, the **Anna Maria Island Historical Museum** promises a memorable visit. Take a leisurely stroll through the museum grounds, and immerse yourself in the beauty and stories that have shaped this idyllic coastal gem.
content_highlights: Historic 1920s schoolhouse setting
Extensive collection of artifacts from early island life
Interactive exhibits for all ages
Guided tours from passionate staff
Insight into the *Cortez Fishing Village* heritage

google_reviews.text:
This place is wonderful and full of knowledgeable staff members and artifacts of Anna Maria's past. We visit from the UK, once in 2022 and again in 2025, our next visit won't be until 2027 sadly. I bought a couple of books there by the founder Carolyne Norwood and have read them cover to cover. Without the upkeep of this history site, its history would be lost. I am very grateful for your work!
This inspired my own book writing of the island and Pine Avenue and this museum will certainly feature prominently!

Very interesting about the history of Anna Maria Island. It's a small museum but backed with information.  Plus they have scavenger hunt for kids and it's free!!! Donations accepted. And there's a small park with a kayak launch too.
We enjoyed the historical Museum It is free to experience and there's a lot of Interesting facts The staff volunteers were very knowledgeable And a pleasure to speak with

What a neat piece of history on the island. The home was once on the end of the pier. After the home was blown into the bay it was moved to another location on the island and remained for 75 years. Truly amazing for a wood structure. Then the community came to the rescue and moved it to its present location on N Shore where it’s available for viewing anytime from the outside or 3 hrs a day during the week. Lots of folks deserve credit for rehabbing the home.  And the jail is original. Pretty cool.

This was a cute little free museum.  Lots of artifacts and history.   There is a tiny gift store, too.  The volunteer working there was super friendly and helpful.   She gave us tips on where to eat that paid off!  The jail is interesting and offers free air conditioning!  Oh and there are some movies that were in part filmed on Anna Maria Island. google_reviews.text:
It’s more an incredible collection of several generations of rich guys’ collectible toys, more than a real museum. Well worth the $20 to wander around.

The most amazing car collection, mostly priceless older vehicles, including an American made Rolls Royce (only done for a few years after WWI).

Lots of interesting info about old Florida (the most museum-ish part), which is relegated to a back corner of the top floor, of course.

A baseball card collection that would have made my 10 year old self have a stroke. Funny how you lose interest in things as you get older. They must have spent a million dollars on all the collectible baseball memorabilia that is fundamentally worthless.

They have a HUGE Fabrige (sp?) Egg collection.

The volunteers are pretty helpful, too.

Not adding all the pictures I took because you should see the museum for yourself. I would highly recommend. I took off two stars because the person by the car section managing the car elevator show case allowed one person before me to request a car be shown from the list. When I wanted to ask he said only the Director can select what cars that section shows. I moved away for a bit to another area and noticed he kept allowing others to select cars. Others could choose but not me? 😞. That really offended me and made me feel bad. The younger generation around my age hardly ever go to museums for fun. I plan my entire vacation around a museum once per year and travel different places in the state specifically to go to the museums. It really made me feel bad. Nevertheless the museum is amazing and I have not been to a car museum before that had such a cool way to display cars. At least I was able to see the cars others picked. My favorite parts were regarding Florida and local history. Specially the book section that had a pictures of the local area in development and seminole indians as I live in FT Lauderdale close to their reservation and casinos. I was in the museum from 12 in the afternoon until almost 5 PM. Awesome place

🏛️ Great museum! Really worth a visit. 1st floor is filled with unusual antique cars and bicycles. Plenty of interesting historical facts about local residents and inventors. 2nd floor is filled with myriad of unique artifacts of Florida history. Most of them are just displayed in a makeshift old store. You can spend hours just exploring this area alone.

🎧 They have an excellent and free audio guide.

🚗 Make sure to check out “car vending machine”. Plus at least two electric cars from 1900s and 1970s. Fun fact, most of their cars are drivable. They rent them to movie studios, news productions, weddings and just take them to auto shows. They have 1930s “Woody” (Ford Model A Staton Wagon) that you can sit in and explore. Make sure you do it and find out just how much more comfortable our cars are today.

🏕️ Moonshine tent display on 2nd floor is excellent.

⏱️ Give yourself ~3-4 hours to explore the museum.

🅿️ There is plenty of free parking in front of the museum. Plus public beach parking right next to the museum.

🍹There is a “Tiki Bar” on site.  If you are hungry, you can visit it too.

🚽 Bathrooms a nice, roomy and very clean.

I was stunned at the amount and quality of their items.  This is an absolute jewel and a must see.  I was not disappointed.  Cost is minimal for the value of seeing great works.  If the docent is available for the cars, ask to see it. They have a racking system unlike anything I've ever seen.   Take your time and take it all in.  I think they have other exhibits that are invited and showcased.  When I visited it was Tut and Faberge eggs replicas.  Active duty and veterans were admitted free with ID at the time of this post. Great way to spend your time.

What a unique place to visit in Stuart.

So many types of exhibits throughout the property, all included in admission fee (general admission (kids 13 yrs to adults under senior age) was $20 per person.  They do have a youth rate and senior and military rate.
Down stairs (floor 1) is a neat pendulum in constant motion right when you enter, various bikes, Florida Highwaymen painting exhibit, antique automobiles, motorcycles, and the vertical vehicle storage machine where the guide will let you choose cars to bring down from different levels and it brings them forward and puts them on a rotational platform where you can view it 360°. Such a cool concept (same as the vertical parking lot creations in crowded cities).
There are also traveling exhibits on display (Egypt- King Tut and Russian Fabergé Eggs (both reproductions but really neat without having to travel to other countries to see) were there while we were visiting in Ddc 2025).  Upstairs on the second floor is a plethora of unique finds.  Planes, boats, bicycles, vintage and antique baseball relics, more paintings, history from the Treasure Coast area, a full antique pharmacy set up and soda fountain. Handmade Wyatt's Circus wooden display (see the video I uploaded). The Ashley Gang exhibit, and so much more.

Family of four, with our two teens and they were really impressed with all of the items we had the pleasure to view.  They do close right at 5pm (or whatever time is advertised) so be ready to spend a few hours looking at everything they have. Staff is super friendly and knowledgeable.  Definitely worth the stop. We didn't try to outside eatery but there is a restaurant on the outside of the building. Plenty of parking and easy to access.

museums.content_description:
**The Elliott Museum** in Stuart rewards the kind of traveler who prefers a museum visit that’s *focused, accessible, and refreshingly local*. Rather than trying to be encyclopedic, the museum leans into a curated approach—rotating exhibitions and changing gallery presentations that often highlight Florida connections, regional creativity, and American cultural history. For art lovers, that means the pleasure of discovery: you may encounter contemporary works by area artists, thematic shows that connect art to place, or tightly edited displays that invite close looking and repeat visits.

Architecturally, the museum reads as **modern and visitor-friendly**, with clean lines, open sightlines, and galleries that encourage an unhurried pace. The overall experience feels intentionally designed for comfort: you can move from one compact, well-organized space to another without fatigue, making it a strong choice for travelers fitting culture into a beach-and-downtown itinerary.

Plan to spend time with the **temporary exhibitions**, which are the museum’s pulse—especially if you enjoy seeing what’s happening *now* in the region’s visual culture. Because the collection is **modest**, the Elliott’s strength is not sheer volume but **curation and context**: exhibitions tend to be approachable, with interpretive materials that help you connect the work to Florida’s history and to broader American artistic currents. If you love museum-going as a way to understand a place, the Elliott makes a compelling, easy-to-savor stop in Stuart.

museums.content_summary: Florida CraftArt is a must for art lovers who want contemporary work with the intimacy and material presence that only craft can deliver. Located in downtown St. Petersburg, this nationally recognized gallery spotlights ambitious exhibitions in ceramics, glass, fiber, wood, jewelry, and mixed media—often with a strong Florida and Southeast perspective. Expect thoughtfully curated shows, a close-up viewing experience, and the chance to meet the region’s makers through events, openings, and an excellent adjacent shop focused on collectable handmade art.
museums.content_description:
**Florida CraftArt** champions the art of the handmade with a contemporary edge, presenting rotating exhibitions that elevate craft as a vital part of today’s visual culture. Rather than a single permanent collection, you’ll encounter a dynamic program centered on ceramics, glass, fiber, wood, metalwork, and jewelry—fields where technique, touch, and experimentation are inseparable from meaning. For visitors, the pleasure is in proximity: you can study glaze surfaces, stitching, tool marks, and joins up close, and follow how artists push materials into sculptural, conceptual, and installation-based territory—an on-the-ground view of *contemporary craft* and *studio practice*.

Set in downtown St. Petersburg, the venue’s gallery layout is designed for careful looking, with clean sightlines that let intricate objects read like sculpture and immersive installations hold the room. The museum’s regional strength is a draw: exhibitions frequently foreground Florida and the broader Southeast, making it an ideal stop for travelers who want a sense of local creative ecosystems—not just a greatest-hits survey.

The visitor experience is welcoming and very “St. Pete”: come for an exhibition, then linger for openings, talks, and community programming that connect you directly to artists and processes. Don’t skip the **Florida CraftArt Shop**, where the curated selection of handmade work makes it easy to take home a piece with real authorship—whether that’s wearable jewelry, small ceramics, or statement objects for the shelf.

This is really a must visit kind of place!  Even if you are not a diver or a technical type, there is some crazy stuff in there you would not believe.  If you are a diver or a tech type (engineer, etc) you HAVE TO visit.
This a specialty museum and it really does a A LOT of history of how humans went underwater on a regular basis.  Much of it is the evolution of the diving bell (diving helmet) which is still used to day for a lot of large underwater construction.  There are sections that talk about the invention, then the industrialization of deep dive suits, then the recreationalization of scuba. There is also a small art gallery the gentleman owner is trying to support local artists.

You can buy a combination ticket to see the Elliott and the House of Refuge museum. I think that is the best deal. You can coordinate for a museum staff member to drive you over and back. It was a good deal and very convenient. I would recommend going to the Elliott first and then the House of Refuge. You could drive yourself but there are very few parking spaces at the Refuge. The house is the only one of the original 10 houses built by Florida to helped shipwrecked people along Florida’s east Coast. You enter through the house by the small parking lot. The staff was very friendly. The entrance house serves as a ticket booth, a waiting area and a gift shop all in one. The small set of structures is located right on the beach and offers a lovely view. They have you start at the third house where a volunteer shows a movie and then describes more about the history of the people and the structures. The next house has individual rooms that describe each period in the history of the house. Overall, it was a very nice visit to a structure that is key in describing the true initial Coast Guard history.

Awesome little piece of history. Well worth a visit. Plan on spending around an hour at the house, and a bit more time walking along the rocky beach. Parking could be tricky, with only around 20 spaces. Pleasant staff who answered questions and were friendly.

The sunrises on this beach are phenomenal and breathtaking.  The rocks and outcroppings are unique to this beach all along the coast of Florida. Small. Quiet. Scenic. Always see photographers capturing wedding couples, children, and families here every morning we come. Worth a visit if you can. No decent swimming but picturesque. Wear stiff shoes. Rocks will cut your feet up.

Not only is the house of refuge the oldest building in Martin County, it’s served as a life-saving service to those that were shipwrecked out on Gilbert‘s bar.

It’s my favorite beach to bring my dogs too. You can see the exposed part of Anastasia‘s formation which is an outcrop of Coquina that was created by polychaete worms. That’s right, a reef system that was built by worms a long, long time ago. And if you catch it at low tide, you can go in front of the worm reef and see all the creatures that inhabited now. My French bulldog Winston loves to explore it.

museums.content_summary: The **House of Refuge** in Stuart offers a captivating glimpse into Florida's maritime history, showcasing the state’s unique coastal heritage within a beautifully preserved 19th-century structure. Visitors experience both history and stunning coastal views, making it a must-see destination for history buffs and nature lovers alike.
museums.content_description:
**The House of Refuge** stands as a remarkable testament to Florida’s storied maritime past. Built in 1876, this historic structure was one of several lifesaving stations along the southeastern coast, designed to aid shipwrecked sailors navigating the perilous waters of the Atlantic. The museum not only serves as a reminder of maritime safety and rescues but is also beautifully located along the picturesque shores of Hutchinson Island. Here, visitors can step back in time and explore the rich history of the *lifesavers* who dedicated their lives to protecting seafarers in distress. Emblematic of the era, the architecture of the house captures Victorian charm, with its wide verandas and expansive ocean views challenging today’s coastal aesthetics. It provides a unique opportunity to appreciate how design intertwined safety with beauty along the coast. 

The museum offers a diverse collection of artifacts, including historical photographs, navigation tools, and everyday items from the time period that narrate the lives of those who worked and lived at the refuge. Interactive exhibits invite visitors to immerse themselves in the stories of shipwrecks and rescues, allowing you to experience the urgency and thrill of maritime rescue missions. Don’t miss the stunning coastal scenery from the property, where the *ocean breeze* and the sound of crashing waves combine with history for an unforgettable visit. The **House of Refuge** not only enriches the understanding of Florida’s maritime history but also inspires a deep appreciation for the natural beauty surrounding it.
content_highlights: 19th-century Victorian architecture
Interactive exhibits on maritime rescues
Beautiful coastal views from the property
Historical artifacts related to the lifesaving station
Unique insight into Florida's coastal heritage

museums.content_description: **Lightner Museum** is an unmissable gem nestled in the historic heart of St. Augustine, Florida. Once the extravagant Hotel Alcazar built in the late 19th century, the museum itself is an architectural marvel, featuring beautiful *Spanish Renaissance* design elements that are sure to enchant visitors. As you step through its grand entrance, you are transported back in time, enveloped by the elegance and grandeur of a bygone era that reflects the unique spirit of America’s Gilded Age. The museum provides a vibrant sanctuary where the past comes alive in captivating ways. The museum is a physical embodiment of luxury and history, with intricately tiled floors, ornate chandeliers, and beautiful courtyards creating an inviting atmosphere that invites exploration. Experience the grandeur from the moment you walk in! In addition to the stunning architectural beauty, the **Lightner Museum** houses an impressive collection of fine art and historical artifacts, including an extensive range of *Victorian* and *Edwardian* antiques, exquisite *European* and *American* paintings, and delightful *Nineteenth-century* glassware. Each piece tells its own story, allowing visitors to dive into the historical and cultural significance of the period. Don’t miss the chance to view their remarkable **silver collection**, which showcases the intricate artistry of craftspeople from a century ago.  Whether you're an art aficionado or a history buff, the **Lightner Museum** promises a delightful journey through time, inviting you to engage and reflect upon the rich tapestry of life in a remarkable era. Don’t forget to stroll through the serene gardens outside, where the beauty of nature complements the artistic treasures within. Plan your visit today and immerse yourself in the historic charm of the **Lightner Museum**!

A great museum, great staff, great grounds. Great experience.

Stunning architecture & historic building: The museum is housed in what was once the luxurious 19th-century Hotel Alcazar — a Gilded-Age resort — and many visitors say the building itself is a major draw. Grand arches, a dramatic courtyard/pool-house converted into exhibit space, ornate staircases and original tile floors create a powerful “stepping back in time” ambiance.
wide variety of items: from cut glass and crystal, to Victorian-era decorative arts, furniture, stained glass, mechanical musical instruments, and more.  the sheer diversity and craftsmanship of these pieces is impressive and.
Rather than a typical museum focused on one theme, Lightner offers what some call a “collection of collections” — a mix of curiosities, antiques, and aesthetic objects that evoke a bygone era. That eclecticism — along with the historic setting — makes it stand out.
Good for a relaxed, flexible visit: Because the museum is in an old hotel with multiple levels and rooms — some accessed by elevator — a stroll through at one’s own pace is possible. Some find this free, unhurried style appealing.
the collections are so varied, some visitors say the museum lacks a cohesive theme or narrative.
Layout can be confusing: The structure — inherited from its hotel-days — can be a bit convoluted.
Lightner Museum is ideal if you enjoy historic architecture, eclectic collections, and curio-style museums rather than polished, highly curated blockbuster exhibits. First off, I love this museum and come back every few years, this year I was sad to see the shrunken head was gone!! We took pictures with it every year! It reminds us of times and cultures and wild places.  Please bring it back!  That was the fun and culture I loved about the museum...having the beautiful antiquities and history and unusual items you will not see anywhere else.

Beautiful building of course - The exhibits were interesting but nothing mind blowing when we visited (check their website for current exhibits).

Very impressive building which was a hotel in another era and housed the largest saltwater pool in the world at one time, part of Henry Flagler's Gilded Age Hotel Alcazar. The pool area is now used for events / weddings.
It’s not like a regular museum but more a gallery of different pieces from the gilded age. Some impressive pieces spread out on different floors accessed by elevators and stairs.
Unique and well worth a visit when in town.

I found the Lightner museum a fascinating collection of odd and interesting displays and objects. The museum is housed in the former Hotel Alcazar, a Gilded Age resort hotel commissioned by Henry Flagler and was built in 1888. The hotel was purchased in 1947 by Otto Lightner a collector who encouraged others to collect anything from matchbox covers to bottlecaps through his magazine callled "Hobbies - the Magazine for Collectors."  He  turned the hotel into a museum for his collections. Many of these items are from the late 19th and early 20th centuries and display an ecletic and interesting variety of items from the Gilded age. I enjoyed the variety and many beautiful items in this museum. I think it is well worth the time to come and enjoy this museum on a visit to St. Augustine.

Located within the Palmetto Historical Park, this museum is easy to pair with a walk through the surrounding historic buildings, making it a great stop for families, history lovers, and anyone curious about how agriculture shaped Manatee County.

One of the biggest highlights is that the museum is **free to enter**, which makes it incredibly accessible and perfect for a spontaneous visit. Despite being small, it is thoughtfully curated and packed with interesting exhibits. The displays explain local agricultural history in a **simple, engaging, and easy-to-follow format**, making it enjoyable for both adults and children. You don’t need to be an expert in farming to appreciate what’s here the information is presented in a way that feels educational without being overwhelming.

The museum includes **multiple buildings**, each focusing on different aspects of farming life, tools, equipment, and pioneer-era practices. There are plenty of hands-on and visual elements that help bring the history to life, and it’s clear a lot of care has gone into preserving these artifacts. Families will especially appreciate the educational resources and activities, which make it a great learning experience for kids.

Another strong point is the **community-focused atmosphere**. These events add energy to the space and make repeat visits worthwhile. google_reviews.text: Absolutely wonderful museum! Victoria is incredibly knowledgeable and answered every question we had about the various pieces and artists. We loved seeing Memphis pieces owned and loved by David Bowie! 10/10 recommend this museum!

If you ever wanted to visit an beutiful Florida town, swing by Mt. Dora Florida.  And check out the Modernism Museum, it is a small Museum could take you 30min to an hour to see everything, but for price its a nice little stop.  Adults are $8 and they do have discount admission for Military, kids and others just ask the desk.  My wife and i went and loved it, they have a few pieces from David Bowe's personal collection.  The gift shop is the reason its only 4 stars.  It was nice, but not alot of items about the Museum itself it did however support local artists so thats a plus.  Afterwards have a walk around town and enjoy a beutiful local florida town.

I really enjoyed my visit here! I ended up buying 2 of their assorted mini materpiece jigsaw puzzles. One of them being my favorite painting starry night, other than one piece being missing from the get go they were really fun to put together!! Will definitely stop by again soon though!

Quite a little gem in Mount Dora. Stopped in and being a kid of the 80s, was fascinated with the Memphis designs. Sure set the stage for the 80s, I hadn't realized the impact on even MTv! Plus some of the pieces came from David Bowie's personal collection. Victoria, the guide was a wealth of information and you could share her enthusiasm.

Really interesting museum in Mount Dora. Memphis design is not my favorite, but I enjoyed the exhibit regardless. I love David Bowie, and seeing his pieces was really cool. Discount at the museum store with your ticket!

The free admission center displays all kinds of art creations by local and international artists. I'm looking forward to the Jan 17 exhibit of pottery by Florida university students.
Wheel chair access throughout.  Heavy door at entrance.  Wheel chair access parking with most spaces pay by app and a few free street spaces with a 2 hour limit.

We had the pleasure of joining Matt in the Hot Shop for a Hot Date class on a Friday night after visiting the Chihuly exhibit. Love this local gem of an art gallery!  Wonderful showcases to be seen here by some talented artists.  Check out the talent they have when you can.  I loved seeing some of the SHINE ON Festival Artists on display & capturing it in a creative, unique way with my glass spheres.

Never a dull moment of creative viewing at this charming establishment with friendly staff!  I'm excited to see what future shows they offer to the public & and the majority of the time is free. I've even been to a cupcake contest and tasting here!  I highly recommend it!
Fun experience! With the price of admission you get to walk through the Chihuly exhibit and then are treated to (if you so choose) a glass blowing demonstration across the street. Very cool!

museums.content_summary: In St. Petersburg’s vibrant Central Arts District, the Morean Arts Center is a must for travelers who want art with a local pulse. Part gallery, part working studio hub, it offers a close-up look at contemporary creativity—especially in glass—plus rotating exhibitions that keep every visit fresh. Come for the chance to watch artists at work, linger with thoughtfully curated shows, and experience a museum atmosphere that feels energetic, welcoming, and deeply connected to the city’s cultural scene.
museums.content_description:
**Morean Arts Center** rewards art lovers who enjoy seeing culture in motion rather than behind velvet ropes. Set in St. Petersburg’s lively arts corridor, it functions as both an exhibition venue and a creative engine—an ideal stop if you’re drawn to *contemporary art* and the ways communities shape it. Instead of a single, fixed “permanent collection” experience, you’ll typically encounter **rotating gallery exhibitions** that spotlight regional and national artists, offering variety across media and a sense of what’s current right now.

A standout strength here is glass. Through the **Chihuly Collection** (part of the Morean’s broader family of sites), visitors can immerse themselves in the dramatic color, scale, and technical bravura associated with Dale Chihuly’s studio practice—an anchor for anyone fascinated by *studio glass* and postwar craft-to-fine-art crossovers. Back at the Arts Center, the appeal is the proximity to process: the programming and educational mission make the visit feel participatory, like stepping into the ecosystem that produces the work.

Architecturally, the experience is urban and walkable, woven into a neighborhood of studios, cafés, and murals—perfect for pairing with a full arts day in St. Pete. Expect an intimate, approachable gallery rhythm: arrive curious, take your time with the temporary shows, and leave feeling plugged into the city’s creative bloodstream.
content_highlights: Rotating contemporary exhibitions that make repeat visits worthwhile
Strong emphasis on glass art through the broader Morean/Chihuly connection
A creative-campus feel with education and community arts at the core
Location in St. Petersburg’s Central Arts District—easy to combine with galleries and murals nearby
An intimate, approachable visitor experience focused on living artists and current work

google_reviews.text: Found this place by accident after taking a wrong turn near Fort Myers Beach, and I’m glad I did. Even though I didn’t go inside, the grounds were beautiful and really well maintained. It’s a peaceful spot and definitely caught my attention. I saw they offer kayak tours, which looked awesome, so I’ll definitely be coming back to check that out and explore the house next time. Worth stopping by if you’re in the area.

Fascinating glimpse into early Florida - not just the early 20th Century but well over 1,000 years into the past. Brianna and Sue explained things very well. The most recent hurricane meant some of the museum is currently under repair, but it's still interesting and informative and gives us something to look forward to on a future visit.
My wife also enjoyed the gift shop.

My child and I recently went on a field trip to Mound House, and it was amazing! It was engaging and educational. The education coordinator and archaeologist were both so wonderful with the kids. I know the kids' favorite part was using the atlatl, but my favorite part was listening to the archaeologist talk about her field work. It's also just a beautiful spot to explore.

Parking outside or if full there is an overflow carpark just before the building,the building has 2 floor with a lift ,the rooms tell you about the history of the building and area around it , upstairs is mainly about archeology about the mound the house was built on.
In the grounds there is a viewing walkway extending into the estuary
Only 10 dollar's admission

We went at a slow time - and didn't have a guided tour. We did have a 25-minute movie on the history of Fort Myers Beach from the Calusa years to about the late 1990s - with great interviews from elderly (in the 1990s) residents who'd lived there their entire life. The house has many exhibits showing life before the Europeans took over - with explanations and artifacts. The grounds have signs about the area, the vegetation, and the history of the house. All-in-all between the movie, the house, and the grounds - we spent about 90 minutes here. There's a small gift shop. And... good views across the water.

google_reviews.text: DO NOT RECOMMEND THE CHILDS ART CAMP. Serious lack of communication and basic safety protocols. Also there was no clear lesson plan and my son spent the entire day coloring on a piece of paper with markers in a single room with folding tables. Enjoyed the art in the alley and saw the current exhibition and live music. And had a nice drink at the Handlebar.
Love MDCA! I love teaching there, showing in the gallery, taking classes and my kids loved the art camp.

This is one of the many reasons that make living in Mount Dora such an amazing experience.

Volunteered here as a teen for the summer arts camp and honestly loved the experience, didn't see much of the lower area, however everything appeared to be set up nicely and organized. Fantastic place to volunteer, and I'm just as confident that the same goes for the art.

google_reviews.text: Very quaint, but a smaller venue. They had a great sampling of various art styles and a wing featuring Latin American artists. They also have materials of what was used, particularly the pink polyurethane tarp.
Absolutely terrific! Exhibit of the Christos Surrounded Islands, well worth a visit. A very impressive feat captured in all the details.GO before it goes the end of February 2026.
I came around mid day during the free first Thursday. Such an interesting and varied collection. Can’t wait to go back for the next one to see their new exhibits.

Visited the Museum in May 2025 , first floor exhibition should have came with a warning of depression , sadness and anxiety. I know art is selective and in the eye of the beholder but seriously it did not give off a good feeling. Lucky on the second floor there was a Haitian artist that was more pleasant to look at . Rather than trying to be encyclopedic, it leans into a carefully edited experience: polished galleries, frequent temporary exhibitions, and an emphasis on artists and ideas shaping the present. The result is a museum that feels current and traveler-friendly—easy to navigate in a single visit, yet substantial enough to linger, revisit, and compare exhibitions over time.

Inside, the collection is **modest but purposeful**, with strengths often framed around art of the Americas and modern-to-contemporary practice. Visitors can expect a lively program of rotating shows that may spotlight *contemporary* painting, photography, and multimedia alongside curated selections from the permanent holdings. The museum’s exhibition schedule is a major draw for art lovers: even if you’ve been before, the galleries often look newly rethought, with interpretive texts and layouts that encourage unhurried viewing and conversation.

Architecturally, the museum reads as a **clean-lined, civic cultural space**—bright, orderly, and designed to keep attention on the art. For travelers, the experience is notably comfortable: manageable gallery scale, a calm pace, and the sense that you’re encountering Orlando’s cultural life beyond theme parks. Pair your visit with nearby cultural venues in the park to make an art-focused afternoon, and check the calendar for **lectures, tours, and special exhibitions** that can turn a simple stop into a deeper encounter.

google_reviews.text:
We visited the Orlando Museum of Art and truly enjoyed the experience. Admission is free the first weekend of each month for Bank of America customers, making it an even better reason to visit.

The museum showcases beautiful works of art, and the current David LaChapelle exhibition was especially impressive and engaging. Be sure to catch a curated tour if available — it was very informative and enhanced the overall visit.

A lovely cultural experience and a great stop for art lovers in the Orlando area.

We went fir the second year in a row to the Festival of Trees. It's always so beautiful to see all the gingerbread houses, wreaths, trees, and tablescapes. Gives us ideas for our own home while being festive. I do feel there was more auction type stuff this year rather than decor but just could've been placement. Really enjoyed!

Enjoyed an evening out on the town listening to a string quartet play legendary songs by The Beatles. We had a lovely time being disconnected (phones on airplane mode) and fully enthralled in the melodies.

There were songs that made my eyes tear up. There were songs that left us in awe. The musicians were lively, introducing the songs with wit and humor, as well as facts about which Beatle had written the song and even the backstory in some cases.

I recommend getting there early, as the email states they do close the doors as to not distract the musicians.

Don't worry, the candles are fake, although delightfully believable. They have them for sale if you care to buy a set for yourself or a loved one.

To our surprise they did offer wine and beer for purchase in the atrium for the duration of the event.

I would go back to see The Beatles cover  for certain, and have already looked into their other offerings around the United States.

Five stars isn’t enough for the experience I had at the Orlando Museum of Art during the David LaChapelle exhibition.

I’ve always loved the Orlando Museum of Art. It has been a place of inspiration for me for years, and I truly appreciate the ways the museum makes art accessible to the community. The free admission days, sketching in the galleries, and other interactive opportunities invite artists and art lovers to slow down, observe, and engage more deeply. Those experiences matter, and they have meant a lot to me over time.

The David LaChapelle exhibition was more than something beautiful to see. It was deeply inspiring and personally meaningful. I’ve followed his work for decades, and experiencing these pieces in person was powerful in a way that images online could never capture. His work reminds us that art isn’t just decoration. It’s emotion, storytelling, and a place to pour your whole self into.

I want to sincerely thank the curator for presenting the collection so thoughtfully and intentionally. The installation allowed each piece to stand on its own while still creating a cohesive journey through his vision.

Thank you to the museum board and the sponsors for investing in an exhibition of this caliber and bringing it to our community. Opportunities like this elevate the local arts scene and inspire working artists like me to keep growing and creating.

And to David LaChapelle himself, thank you for sharing your vision with the world and for creating work that continues to challenge, inspire, and remind artists why we fell in love with art in the first place. It was such an honor to meet such a master of photography.

This exhibition was unforgettable, and I’m incredibly grateful that Orlando had the opportunity to experience it.

Side note: As a wedding photographer, I also want to add that the Orlando Museum of Art is a stunning venue for weddings and receptions. The architecture, natural light, and artistic atmosphere create a unique and elegant setting that makes celebrations feel truly special. If you are looking to book something unique, this is the venue!

A wonderful display of global and local art. Some of the most vivid and beautiful array of watercolor paintings. Along with inspiring contributions from local schools OMA is must visit for lovers and the casual admirer of the arts.

google_reviews.text:
This art gallery currently has some interesting but very disturbing works on display (August 2025). I couldn’t quite understand the motivation behind the exhibition, which felt more suited to a dedicated contemporary art venue.. especially because the pieces have such a provoking character. The “Duality” exhibition on the second floor was intense.

For example, one piece showed a twisted, uprooted tree hanging from above, and beneath it a torn-up patch of grass resembling a grave, where several maggots were arranged around two dead hands. This is not for children… my son, looking at it, couldn’t understand what he was seeing.

Personally, I also found the “church tank” and some hanging udders difficult to take in within the context of a city museum. I don’t feel that the Museum of Art is the right environment for these works, and I wouldn’t take my kids back here.

Ticket: We got a combined ticket for the Museum of History, the Art Gallery, and the Historic Village.. $12 for adults and $7 for kids. It’s a good deal if you want a first look into Pensacola’s culture and history all in one day.

Museum Store: yes

Very small, very personal exhibition with a few nice pieces and a historic setting inside and old jail. The centerpiece down stairs was basically the highlight of the trip. The lady at the front desk was nice and sociable and there was an art class during my visit that was full underway.

Art Mueseum is small went through it in about 30 min. You also get admission to the History, Industry, Commerce and Childrens Museums plus a tour through the Historic Church and Homes they offer 3 times a day.

Admittedly, the museum is small, and its current layout may feel limited. At the moment, only one floor is open, mainly showcasing local or regional contemporary creations, which may not appeal to all visitors. There is a small engraving by Goya and a piece by Gallé, though these are discreetly placed and easy to overlook.

I remembered, from a visit about twenty years ago, a respectable collection of 19th-century American paintings that I found of real interest. It's unclear whether this has been moved or replaced temporarily, possibly to make room for the upcoming exhibition (apparently focused on aquatic themes, based on what's being prepared upstairs).

Of course, this is only a matter of personal taste. I hope that the museum’s promise of being “more than a museum,” as stated on the poster outside, will be realized in future exhibitions. For now, I personally found the current offering rather underwhelming. The French-language signage is somewhat tucked away in a back corridor, currently closed to children’s activities.

That said, the staff were very welcoming, admission was reduced (6 instead of 12 dollars), and the ticket is valid for a week and also gives access to other museums in the city—which is a definite plus. The temperature inside, thanks to the building's history as a former prison, is pleasantly cool.

3/27/2025: Small art museum in the historic district of Pensacola. I’m not a big art gallery person, but this self guided tour was part of the full ticket we purchased, so we checked it out while we were there. It took us about 25 minutes to see all the exhibits. It’s worth the time to check it out.

The Sarasota Art Museum occupies a former school building. It is run by the Ringling School of Art and Design, and it is a non-collecting Museum. It features special exhibits on three floors. I was not sure about visiting, but I was VERY HAPPY to have stopped by. There is a lot of exhibition space, plenty of parking, an awesome cafe, and a wonderful gift shop. The special exhibition on Art Deco era posters is superb. It is a private collection featuring advertising employed in the 30s using poster art. Themes include travel, vehicles, and vices. It is quite impressive and it occupies👍the entire third floor. The other key exhibit features large scale exhibits using string like material to create giant suspended art. The artist also does abstract art featuring unique colors.
This museum is only about a half mile from downtown Sarasota. I was impressed with the high quality of the exhibits, and the facility itself is well done considering that it was once a school. Also check out some of the outdoor sculptures. There are a few permanent pieces of artwork. Absolutely make sure to see the mounted dishware artwork on both the first and second floors. You must walk all the way to the northern end of the building to see it!

We started our visit with a lunch in the museum bistro which is a lovely airy place to eat and while away some time. There is also an informative display about the history of the Thonet chair.
We are from the Uk and were interested to hear that the Sarasota art museum was hosting an Art Deco posters exhibition. We love to visit the many wonderful art galleries when we visit Florida. The poster exhibition is vast and very informative. We enjoyed it immensely. Jude one of the curators made it extra special for us with her knowledge not only of the posters but the local area too.
An excellent facility, well worth a visit. When we visited an Art Deco poster exhibition was running which I highly recommend. Try the Bistro too, we had a wonderful lunch with great service.

Three floors of great exhibits! Love the use of  the light streaming through the windows! Three floors of stunning art! This was my first visit - second Sundays are FREE! Incredible flamenco musician -  brought tears to my eyes!! Also a talented vocalist!

This will be a regular stop for me!

We visited the museum during our Christmas break weekend trip to Tampa… my daddy was interested in going there! The museum is a cool place to visit, and when we got there, the staff let us take our 1-strap purses in, even though it says that bags with backpack straps (particularly large bags) are not permitted and must be put in a locker or left in your vehicle.
The special exhibit has cool surrealist art and sculptures, and there is an interactive area called the “Endless Garden”, where you can scan a QR code, answer a few questions, and watch your ideas and designs appear on the big screen! My idea that took shape was a surreal flower with insect legs.
The regular gallery (with Dali’s permanent artwork) also has a cool feature when you use augmented reality and see some of the artworks come to life.
The outdoor area is so beautiful, with sculptures (like a little bird with a Dali mustache), a tree where people leave their wristbands hanging, and a big dome-shaped theater. We didn’t get to go in the theater because we just came here to look at the art, but it’s still fun!
The gift shop has a HUGE selection of souvenirs inspired by Dali and his artwork, and the cafe has fancy food and drinks. I got an orange Fanta bottle as my drink and some crème brûlée as my snack.
I highly recommend visiting this place, as the Tampa-St. Petersburg area is not far from our house (about a 5 hr 30 min drive)!

The Dali Museum in St. Petersburg, FL, is an absolute must-visit! The museum houses an impressive collection of Salvador Dali’s surreal and imaginative works, from paintings to sculptures, all thoughtfully displayed. The architecture of the building is stunning, with modern design and beautiful waterfront views that make the visit even more memorable. The exhibits are engaging and informative, giving you a deeper appreciation of Dali’s genius. Whether you’re an art enthusiast or just looking for a unique experience, this museum is well worth the trip!

I also had a delish tiramisu coffee drink and enjoy the walk outside.

Hands down, this is the best art museum I’ve ever visited.

The artwork here is presented in a way that is completely unlike a traditional museum. The Dalí Museum has embraced modern technology to create a deeply immersive experience rather than just static viewing.

Several paintings are enhanced with augmented reality—you simply use your phone camera and watch the artwork come to life. There are VR headsets that let you explore Dalí’s world in virtual reality. Unfortunately, the VR setup isn’t well equipped to handle prescription glasses, which was a bit of a bummer for me. That said, I was still able to enjoy the experience—everything blurred equally well, and I genuinely appreciated the creative use of this modern technology.

There’s also an AI-powered experience that brings your “dream” to life in the form of art, which felt both playful and very Dalí-esque.

I also did the dome immersive experience focused on Vincent van Gogh. While it wasn’t as impressive as the Dalí experiences, it did help me understand Van Gogh more as a person, which added some value.

If you want the full experience and don’t want to rush, plan to spend 3–4 hours here. This museum truly sets a new benchmark for how art can be experienced in the modern age.

I’m not usually someone who gets excited about museums. Having lived in Boston and Los Angeles, I’ve visited many of the country’s most well-known institutions, so my expectations tend to be high.

The Dalí Museum pleasantly surprised me.

The visit reminded me of the true purpose of a museum: to inspire, educate, and encourage reflection. Despite being familiar with Salvador Dalí’s work, I realized I knew very little about his personal life and artistic philosophy.

The exhibits were informative, but the highlight was the auditorium film about Dalí’s life and perspective. It provided valuable insight into his thinking and added meaningful context to the artwork.

While the museum itself isn’t especially large or grand, it offers a thoughtful and engaging experience. If you enjoy learning, reflection, and understanding the artist behind the work, this is a worthwhile visit.

We attended a wedding here, and the entire experience was incredible. The museum itself is a work of art, from the striking architecture to the beautiful waterfront views. Every angle feels intentional, interesting, and visually impressive.

The staff was wonderful- they were professional, welcoming, and attentive, which made the event run seamlessly. One of the coolest parts was walking around the museum during the reception and viewing the art collections. Experiencing Dalí’s work in such an intimate, relaxed setting made it feel even more special and immersive.

Between the breathtaking views, the fascinating architecture, and the world-class art, it was an unforgettable venue and overall experience. Whether you’re visiting for the art or considering it as an event space, this museum is truly something special. A great wedding, a beautiful venue, and an experience we’ll always remember.

museums.content_summary: The **Dalí Museum** in St. Petersburg offers an unforgettable journey through the surreal world of Salvador Dalí, showcasing the largest collection of his artwork outside of Spain. Its striking architecture and immersive exhibits provide a captivating experience for both art lovers and curious travelers alike.
museums.content_description: **The Dalí Museum** is a breathtaking homage to one of the 20th century's most influential artists, Salvador Dalí. Nestled in the scenic waterfront of St. Petersburg, Florida, this museum houses the most extensive collection of Dalí's works outside of Spain, including over 2,000 pieces ranging from paintings and drawings to sculptures and photographs. The museum's unique architectural design features a stunning glass and concrete structure, which harmoniously blends modernity with the imaginative spirit of Dalí's *surrealism*. Upon entering, visitors are greeted by a breathtaking atrium filled with lush gardens, creating a tranquil oasis that contrasts wonderfully with the vibrant energy of Dalí's artistry.  An unforgettable experience awaits as you wander through themed galleries that not only showcase his iconic works but also illuminate the evolution of his artistic journey and fascination with themes like dreams and the subconscious.  The thoughtful curation allows visitors to engage with Dalí’s profound reflections on art and life, fostering a deeper appreciation for his eccentric genius.  Alongside the permanent collection, the museum frequently hosts temporary exhibitions that delve into various aspects of art and culture, ensuring there’s always something new to explore.  The visitor experience is further enhanced by the interactive programs and guided tours that provide insights into the complex layers of Dalí’s work, making it accessible even for those new to art. For a truly immersive dive into a *surreal* dream world, the **Dalí Museum** is a must-visit destination for anyone traveling to St. Petersburg.

Stunning glass and concrete architectural design
Interactive exhibits and immersive programs
Beautiful gardens in a serene atrium

Architecturally, VBMA reads as a calm, Florida-appropriate cultural campus: clean lines, daylight-friendly spaces, and a scale that keeps you close to the art. Check the calendar before you go—at a museum like this, the temporary shows are often the headline—then plan time for the shop and any public talks or tours that may be running during your stay.

museums.content_summary: Nestled in the heart of the Big Cypress Reservation, the **Ah-Tah-Thi-Ki Museum** offers an immersive exploration of the rich culture and history of the Seminole Tribe of Florida. This unique museum not only showcases art and artifacts but also provides a deep connection to the stories and traditions that shape the identity of the tribe today. A visit here promises an educational and meaningful experience for all ages.
museums.content_description: **Ah-Tah-Thi-Ki Museum**, located in Clewiston, Florida, stands as a tribute to the vibrant culture and enduring spirit of the Seminole Tribe. The museum’s name translates to “a place to learn” in the Seminole language, perfectly encapsulating its mission to educate visitors about the tribe’s heritage. This unique facility is not just a collection of artifacts; it is an immersive experience that bridges the gap between past and present, showcasing the importance of preserving indigenous culture. The museum features an extensive collection of historical and contemporary Seminole art, clothing, and tools, all meticulously curated to tell the story of resilience and innovation among the tribe members. Here, you will discover the significance of traditional crafts, the art of storytelling, and the ceremonial practices that have sustained the Seminole community through generations. Discover the traditional *patchwork quilts* and intricate *basket weaving* techniques that reflect both artistry and utility. In addition, the museum includes a stunning outdoor walking trail that surrounds a peaceful, natural environment, inviting contemplation and connection to the land. Guided tours and frequent cultural demonstrations enhance the visitor experience, allowing guests to engage directly with tribal members and learn firsthand about their customs and practices. With a commitment to education, preservation, and cultural exchange, the **Ah-Tah-Thi-Ki Museum** is a place where visitors not only observe but participate in the living legacy of the Seminole Tribe of Florida. Whether you're an art enthusiast, history buff, or just curious traveler, this museum promises a memorable journey into a rich cultural landscape.
content_highlights: Extensive collection of Seminole art and artifacts
Engaging outdoor walking trail with natural surroundings
Cultural demonstrations by Seminole tribal members
Interactive exhibits showcasing traditional crafts
Educative programs aimed at preserving indigenous culture

Five stars isn’t enough for the experience I had at the Orlando Museum of Art during the David LaChapelle exhibition.

I’ve always loved the Orlando Museum of Art. It has been a place of inspiration for me for years, and I truly appreciate the ways the museum makes art accessible to the community. The free admission days, sketching in the galleries, and other interactive opportunities invite artists and art lovers to slow down, observe, and engage more deeply. Those experiences matter, and they have meant a lot to me over time.

The David LaChapelle exhibition was more than something beautiful to see. It was deeply inspiring and personally meaningful. I’ve followed his work for decades, and experiencing these pieces in person was powerful in a way that images online could never capture. His work reminds us that art isn’t just decoration. It’s emotion, storytelling, and a place to pour your whole self into.

I want to sincerely thank the curator for presenting the collection so thoughtfully and intentionally. The installation allowed each piece to stand on its own while still creating a cohesive journey through his vision.

Thank you to the museum board and the sponsors for investing in an exhibition of this caliber and bringing it to our community. Opportunities like this elevate the local arts scene and inspire working artists like me to keep growing and creating.

And to David LaChapelle himself, thank you for sharing your vision with the world and for creating work that continues to challenge, inspire, and remind artists why we fell in love with art in the first place. It was such an honor to meet such a master of photography.

This exhibition was unforgettable, and I’m incredibly grateful that Orlando had the opportunity to experience it.

Side note: As a wedding photographer, I also want to add that the Orlando Museum of Art is a stunning venue for weddings and receptions. The architecture, natural light, and artistic atmosphere create a unique and elegant setting that makes celebrations feel truly special. If you are looking to book something unique, this is the venue!

A wonderful display of global and local art. Some of the most vivid and beautiful array of watercolor paintings. Along with inspiring contributions from local schools OMA is must visit for lovers and the casual admirer of the arts.

Nestled along the banks of the Caloosahatchee River, this historic site features the winter homes of Thomas Edison and Henry Ford. Both structures, designed in a *Mediterranean Revival* style, are surrounded by lushly landscaped gardens filled with tropical plants, providing a serene backdrop that transports visitors back in time. The estates showcase an impressive collection of artifacts, including Edison's early inventions and Ford's iconic automobiles, illustrating their contributions to innovation and industry. Overall, it’s a worthwhile stop—especially for anyone interested in innovation, American industry, or Florida history. It strikes a solid balance between preservation and accessibility. I would absolutely recommend it to visitors in the Fort Myers area.

museums.content_summary: In Fort Pierce, the A.E. Backus Museum of Art is a rewarding stop for anyone who loves American landscape painting and Florida’s visual history. Centered on the work and legacy of “Florida’s Highwaymen” forerunner A.E. Backus, the museum celebrates the luminous skies, rivers, and wetlands of the Treasure Coast. Expect an intimate, regional museum experience—thoughtful exhibitions, a strong sense of place, and a visit that connects art directly to the surrounding environment.
museums.content_description:
**A.E. Backus Museum of Art** is a small but resonant destination for art lovers tracing Florida’s cultural landscape through painting. Dedicated to Albert Ernest “A.E.” Backus (1906–1990)—a pivotal figure in Florida landscape art and an important influence on the later *Florida Highwaymen*—the museum foregrounds the region’s waterways, palm-lined horizons, and changing light. You’ll typically encounter atmospheric oils and works on paper that translate the Treasure Coast into color: glowing sunsets, expansive skies, and wetlands rendered with confident brushwork and a strong sense of local identity.

The museum’s strength lies in its **regional focus**. Rather than attempting an encyclopedic survey, it offers rotating exhibitions and collection presentations that deepen appreciation for Florida’s artistic lineage—especially *plein-air* approaches and American landscape traditions as they evolved in the state. For visitors, that means a clear, coherent narrative: how artists pictured Florida, how tourism and development shaped imagery, and why Backus’s vision became a touchstone.

Architecturally and experientially, expect a **welcoming, human-scale gallery environment** that rewards slow looking. The visit pairs well with exploring Fort Pierce’s historic downtown and waterfront; the paintings often make you notice the real sky and water differently when you step back outside. It’s an ideal museum for travelers who prefer focused collections, regional discovery, and the quiet pleasure of seeing a place “through the artist’s eyes.”
content_highlights: A.E. Backus landscapes capturing the Treasure Coast—rivers, wetlands, and dramatic Florida skies
Context for Florida’s landscape tradition, including Backus’s role as a key predecessor to the Florida Highwaymen
Rotating exhibitions that spotlight regional artists and themes tied to local environment and history
An intimate, easy-to-navigate museum scale that encourages close viewing and repeat visits
A visit that pairs naturally with Fort Pierce’s waterfront scenery—see the painted light, then step into it outside

museums.content_summary: Gainesville’s Harn Museum of Art is one of Florida’s most rewarding university art museums—calm, carefully curated, and surprisingly wide-ranging. You’ll move from luminous Asian ceramics to African sculpture, from modern and contemporary works to thoughtfully presented decorative arts, all in a light-filled building designed for unhurried looking. With changing exhibitions, strong teaching-museum energy, and a welcoming setting on the University of Florida campus, the Harn is a smart stop for art lovers seeking depth without crowds.
museums.content_description:
**The Harn Museum of Art** (University of Florida) is a regional standout for travelers who love museums that feel both *scholarly* and refreshingly accessible. As a university museum, it excels at clear interpretation—labels that actually help you look—and a steady rhythm of rotating exhibitions that keep repeat visits worthwhile. The curatorial approach is **competent and thoughtful**, favoring focused presentations over sheer volume, so you’re rarely overwhelmed and often surprised by smart juxtapositions across time and geography.

Collection-wise, the Harn’s strength is its **global breadth**: you can spend real time with **Asian art** (often a visitor favorite for ceramics and sculpture), explore **African art** with an emphasis on material presence and cultural context, and then pivot into **modern and contemporary art** where ideas about form, identity, and experimentation take center stage. Because the permanent holdings are modest, the museum leans into *connoisseurship-by-selection*—highlighting standout objects and using exhibitions to deepen particular themes rather than trying to be encyclopedic.

Architecturally, expect a **bright, contemplative museum experience**: galleries designed for slow looking, comfortable pacing, and natural-feeling transitions between collection areas. For art-focused travelers, this is the kind of museum where you can visit for 60–90 minutes and leave feeling genuinely enriched—then linger a bit longer for special exhibitions, educational programming, or simply the pleasure of a well-made space devoted to seeing.
content_highlights: Global scope in an intimate format: Asian, African, modern and contemporary art presented with strong interpretation
Asian art galleries often anchored by ceramics and sculpture—ideal for close looking at glaze, surface, and form
African art displays emphasizing materials and object presence, with contextual framing suited to curious visitors
Rotating exhibitions that refresh the museum regularly and reward repeat visits
Light-filled, contemplative gallery design that supports a calm, unhurried viewing experience on the University of Florida campus

google_reviews.text: Located on the University of Florida campus this art museum is a cool free activity to do. After the event, we toured the museum which is a little small but seems like will be much larger after construction. It has many large pieces and smaller rooms to explore different exhibits. There is an outdoor waterfall type area and a rock garden (which is currently closed) to get some fresh air between the exhibits. Parking is free on weekends and after 3:30 on weekdays. The museum itself was nice, but coming in off of Natural Area Rd or Citrus Rd (The back way I guess you could call it) there were no clear signs stating that you needed a parking pass to park in the lot. There was a small sign that said something about how parking is free after 3:30pm or $4 in the parking structure, but when we came in that is the only sign we saw. We spent maybe 30-45min inside before leaving. We got to our vehicle and found a parking ticket for $35 due to “no parking pass”. I was frustrated as most would be but then I started to see other yellow envelopes. We went up and down two lanes before leaving the property and saw that the meter maid had given out 10 other tickets not including mine, and those are only the ones we saw, I’m sure there were many more we missed. The lot wasn’t huge so 11 tickets was a good percentage of the lot. I would have had no problem paying the $4 to park in the structure if there had been more clear signage that stated you needed a pass to park in the open lot. It’s very OBVIOUS to me that it is not clearly posted that you need a parking pass. It’s obvious because a minimum of 10 other people also got tickets, so what does that tell you. I highly doubt 10+ people decided to dodge a few dollar parking fee. $35 a pop, that’s $385 MINIMUM they made off of their patrons in a 45min time span. I would like to be clear that there were many signs of you come in off of Hull Rd, but only 1 bent sign that you will most likely miss if you come in off Natural Area or Citrus Rd. The whole thing seems like a scam to me which is disappointing. Like I said, a MINIMUM of 11 tickets were issued within less than an hour, I’m sure the number was higher, 11 is all that we counted going down only 2 lanes.It’s a disgusting practice and I will NOT be returning to this museum anytime soon. museums.content_description:
**Revs Institute for Automotive Research** is not just a museum; it is a journey through the fascinating world of automotive history. Located in the heart of the automotive innovation landscape, this institute houses a meticulously curated collection of classic and significant vehicles, which serve as a testament to the evolution of automotive design and technology. Visitors are treated to a rare opportunity to experience some of the world’s most iconic cars, meticulously restored and preserved for future generations to admire. These automobiles are not merely machines; they represent the artistry of masterful engineers, the thrill of racing, and the cultural milestones of their respective eras. 

The architecture of the **Revs Institute** itself is as captivating as the exhibits within. The museum's design cleverly melds modern aesthetics with the vintage charm of classic automobiles, offering guests a comfortable space to appreciate the artistry behind the vehicles. Interactive displays and engaging resources provide an educational experience, making it easy for visitors of all ages to grasp the significant advancements in automotive technology and design over the decades. Whether you're a dedicated car enthusiast or simply curious about the influence of cars on modern society, the **Revs Institute** promises an inspiring journey through the fascinating narrative of automobile history, leaving you with a renewed appreciation for these remarkable machines.

This captivating destination boasts over 5,000 works of art, ranging from *Old Masters* to *contemporary pieces*, all housed within an 18th-century Italian Renaissance-style villa. Visitors are welcomed into an environment where *artistic expression* weds beautifully with lush landscapes, offering a tranquil experience unlike any other in the area. The museum’s gardens, designed in the early 20th century, are a masterpiece in themselves, featuring an array of *seasonal blooms*, serene water features, and a picturesque layout that invites you to wander and enjoy the stillness of nature. These botanical gardens reflect the historical significance of their design and provide a peaceful retreat for all who visit.  

In addition to the stunning visuals within the gardens, the museum hosts a series of educational programs and exhibitions that engage visitors of all ages. Families can participate in artist-led workshops, while solo visitors may find inspiration in the ever-changing exhibits that showcase both regional and international artists. Interactive opportunities are available throughout the museum, including guided tours that deepen your understanding of the art and its contextual relevance within history. Whether you are an art aficionado or simply seeking a serene escape, **The Cummer Museum of Art and Gardens** promises a stimulating experience where you can lose yourself in beauty and creativity.

5,000+ works of art spanning centuries
Beautifully designed botanical gardens with seasonal blooms
Educational programs and artist-led workshops

The Ashley Gibson Barnett Museum of Art, “The AGB” for short, is formerly known as the Polk Museum of Art (and probably what I’ll always think of it as). The name change came with a huge expansion which allowed the museum to nearly thrills its exhibition and learning spaces. Polk County & Lakeland truly have something to be proud of with this museum. And the best part? Free admission!! I wasn’t sure if it’d remain this way after their buildout but they are striving to keep it free for all to visit and enjoy.

They have a really impressive collection for being a still smaller museum compared to the Met, Chicago Museum of Art or places like that. First, you walk into to see several Auguste Rodin sculptures, starting off strong. You can see Andy Warhol, an incredible mix of diverse artists from all over the world, and even a few Dale Chihuly blown glass pieces. It is all absolutely stunning.

The AGB is a Smithsonian affiliate so they definitely have high standards. museums.content_description:
**Pérez Art Museum Miami** (PAMM) is a beacon of contemporary art, set against the stunning backdrop of Biscayne Bay. Opened in 2013, this museum is not only a premier venue for modern and contemporary works but also a masterpiece of architectural design. Created by the renowned firm Herzog & de Meuron, the building itself is an *artistic statement*, showcasing innovative *sustainable features* and integrating seamlessly with its natural surroundings. The lush, hanging gardens and expansive terraces invite visitors to immerse themselves in both art and nature, enhancing their overall experience.  

Inside, PAMM's thoughtfully curated exhibitions feature an impressive array of over 2,000 works from artists across the globe, with a particular emphasis on Latin American and Caribbean art. Visitors can explore vibrant installations and thought-provoking pieces that challenge norms and provoke conversation. The museum also hosts a variety of educational programs and community outreach, making art accessible to all. A visit is more than just viewing art; it's an invitation to engage with the voices and narratives of an ever-evolving global art scene.  

After exploring the galleries, guests can relax at the museum’s café, enjoying breathtaking views of the waterfront while sampling delicious local cuisine. The **Pérez Art Museum** transcends the traditional museum experience, immersing visitors in the soul of Miami's art scene through an unforgettable blend of architecture, collections, and cultural engagement.
content_highlights: Extensive collection of Latin American and Caribbean contemporary art
Architectural masterpiece designed by Herzog & de Meuron
Stunning views of Biscayne Bay from the museum's terraces
Innovative exhibitions that engage with modern themes and societal issues
Dynamic educational programs and community events

google_reviews.text:
Visiting the Pérez Art Museum Miami was truly an inspiring experience, a place where art, nature, and the city’s energy come together beautifully.

The latest exhibits feel thoughtfully curated, with modern Latin American art present in nearly every corner. Each gallery encourages reflection while still feeling vibrant and accessible, making the experience enjoyable whether you’re an art enthusiast or simply curious to explore.

One of the highlights was the immersive chromatic experience inspired by Carlos Cruz-Diez. Walking through the installation feels like stepping inside color itself, light shifts, tones evolve, and your perception changes with every step. It’s playful, modern, and deeply engaging, creating a sensory experience that stays with you long after you leave the room.

Beyond the galleries, the open-air patio overlooking the Bay might be one of Miami’s most relaxing cultural spaces. Watching boats glide by while feeling the ocean breeze makes you want to sit back, unwind, and simply enjoy the moment under the sun.

The iconic hanging swings are a highlight on their own, perfect for strolling, relaxing, and taking in the view. It’s an ideal spot for families, kids, or anyone wanting to pause between exhibits and recharge while surrounded by nature.

Another fun fact is the inspiration for its construction, representing the historic Stiltsville houses, which beautifully resemble the wooden structures built over the water during the Prohibition era, once used as offshore gathering spots where alcohol was served beyond mainland restrictions. The setup captures both nostalgia and Miami’s unique coastal history, adding another layer of storytelling to the visit.

Overall, the Pérez Art Museum Miami is more than a museum, it’s an experience. Between immersive art, stunning waterfront views, and thoughtfully designed spaces to relax, it offers the perfect balance of culture and leisure. Whether you come for the exhibits, the architecture, or simply to enjoy a peaceful afternoon by the bay, it’s a place that invites you to stay longer than planned.

I went to The Bass with my husband and 11-year-old son today on one of their Family Fun Days when they have free admission on the last Sunday of the month. Everything was going well. The exhibits were really nice.

It would have been a 5-star experience had it not been for one of the museum staff who was kind of rude with us. It was when we were leaving- we bought two chips and a soda from the little cafe they have inside near the exit/entrance. We saw that there was a gallery on the other side that we had missed (the Jack Pierson one). We were about to enter when the staff stopped us and said we had to finish our snacks before entering. We had no problem doing that.

Actually, what we had decided to do was for me to go in the gallery with my son while my husband waited outside in the lobby. My husband was about to place the snacks we bought on a table that was nearby. The staff member stopped him and said that the table was being used for registering kids for classes. There were no other kids nearby and also no one who was even near the table.

Anyway, we obliged. While I was inside the gallery with my son, the staff member pretty much followed us like a hound and it was, honestly, really scary. This happened when we went inside a room to watch a video- the staff member immediately followed us. We were not doing anything wrong, only looking at the exhibits. I felt very uncomfortable, intimidated, and honestly, quite afraid. So I took my son and we rushed through viewing all the exhibits in that section. Even my son was feeling uncomfortable and when we came back to the front to meet with my husband, he could immediately tell something was off.

I understand museum policies and everything and respect them. However, our chips weren’t even open and we would have finished our soda in less than a minute. The way the staff member approached us was just quite hostile. Maybe having signs that say anything purchased in the cafe must be left outside even if unopened. And then there was the fact that we were literally being followed while going through the gallery.

We were the only ones there at the time. Looking back, I wonder if I was intentionally targeted and profiled based on the fact that we were brown (South Asian) people. The vibes were off and never have I felt so scared of a museum employee before.

It’s a shame because, besides the one employee who needs to be trained about racial profiling and not stalking museum patrons to the point where they are about to have a panic attack , the museum is great and a 5-star experience.

Like all art, the enjoyment you're going to get out of the museum is subjective. There were a few exhibits and artists I enjoyed but most of it just didn't connect with me, felt too hodgepodge. Baker Museum stands not just as a repository of artistic brilliance but as a testament to the power of generosity, where the joy of experiencing art is generously extended to all who walk through its doors

museums.content_summary: Set on the shores of Lake Formosa in a converted lakeside home, the Mennello Museum of American Art offers a focused, intimate encounter with American art—especially work rooted in Florida’s creative identity. It’s best known for its outstanding holdings of folk-modern painter Earl Cunningham, alongside rotating exhibitions that spotlight regional voices and wider American themes. Come for the calm galleries, the sculpture garden atmosphere, and a visit that feels personal rather than overwhelming—an art-lover’s refuge minutes from downtown Orlando.
museums.content_description:
**Mennello Museum of American Art** is one of Orlando’s most rewarding small museums: a place where American art feels close-up and human-scaled. Housed in a charming former residence on Lake Formosa, the museum pairs **domestic architecture** with a carefully edited presentation, creating an experience more like visiting a collector’s home than a blockbuster institution. The setting—water views, mature trees, and a quiet neighborhood feel—helps frame the museum’s mission to connect visitors to American creativity with an emphasis on Florida’s cultural landscape.

The museum’s signature strength is its significant collection of works by **Earl Cunningham**, whose exuberant, densely patterned paintings bridge *folk* sensibility and a modernist eye for rhythm, color, and flattened space. Seeing Cunningham in depth is a rare pleasure: recurring motifs, bold palettes, and imaginative scenes reveal an artist who defies easy categorization. Beyond the permanent core, expect **rotating exhibitions** that mix regional and national perspectives—often pairing contemporary approaches with historical context—making repeat visits worthwhile.

For travelers, the appeal is the **unhurried visitor experience**: approachable galleries, thoughtful labels, and an easy flow between indoor viewing and outdoor pauses. Plan time to linger on the grounds and take in the museum’s lakeside calm; it’s an ideal counterpoint to Orlando’s larger attractions, offering a quiet, art-centered interlude with strong local character.
content_highlights: Significant holdings of Earl Cunningham paintings, a standout in Florida-focused American art
Intimate galleries in a converted lakeside home—close viewing and a personal scale
Rotating exhibitions that spotlight regional artists alongside broader American themes
Lake Formosa setting that encourages a slow, reflective visit before or after the galleries
A manageable, art-lover-friendly stop near downtown Orlando—easy to pair with other cultural sites
